newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: MAJOR OIL FIRMS LOOK AT IVORIAN DEEPWATER DEPOSITS.
newsitem.headline: MAJOR OIL FIRMS LOOK AT IVORIAN DEEPWATER DEPOSITS.

text.p: Ivory Coast's new hydrocarbons code is enticing major oil firms like Shell to look at oil and gas exploration in its deep-water areas, eight years after one big firm gave up its work in shallower waters, officials say.
"Shell is here to discuss a production-sharing contract for block CI-105 in association with UMIC," mines and energy minister Lamine Fadika told a news conference on Thursday.
"It is a big event for Ivory Coast because it is our first deep-water block. Up until now we have explored and exploited blocks under 200 metres deep," he said.
UMIC, part of Houston-based United Meridian Corp , is the main operator of the Lion and Panthere fields in near-shore block CI-11, Ivory Coast's only productive fields at the moment.
They yield about 20,000 barrels of oil a day and enough gas to fire a power station that has helped the country become a net exporter of electricity.
The government is aiming to further diversify Ivory Coast's cocoa-based economy by heavy promotion of its mineral resources.
"Studies have shown Ivory Coast has important hydrocarbon deposits in shallow water, but at greater depths we have bigger quantities -- billions of barrels of oil," Fadika said.
He said a new hydrocarbons code adopted last month helped compensate for high exploration costs in deep-water offshore areas by giving extra incentives like extended permit validity.
"This policy has been put into action and today I have in Abidjan four groups in discussion with us, above all Shell."
"A second group is here for the development of Espoir, which was operated by Phillips (Petroleum Co ). A series of unfavourable factors caused Phillips to shut up shop," he said.

Phillips produced about 31 million barrels of oil and 62 billion cubic feet of gas in the mid 1980s but it abandoned the field in 1988 due to low oil prices, high operating costs and a policy of withdrawing from the region.
Fadika said Austrian state firm OMV AG and Swiss-based Addax Petroleum, a fully owned subsidiary of the Addax and Oryx group, wanted to redevelop Espoir and explore the rest of block CI-26.
Addax signed a production-sharing deal with the government last December and it plans to produce 100 million barrels of oil and 200 billion cubic feet of gas during the life of the field.
It says the block has seven exploration prospects outside the Espoir area, three in very deep water of 500-1,500 metres.

Block CI-24, which contains the Belier field, was also the subject of renewed interest, Fadika told reporters. Shell and the Santa Fe and Orion groups from the United States were in discussions with the government, he said.
The next deal to be signed, however, is likely to be with U.S. firm Global Natural Resources for block CI-104.
"In principle if there is no problem with the negotiations we will be signing the production-sharing agreement in the Prime Minister's office tomorrow," Fadika said.
